canberra.title: ‘Cowboy culture’ claim: CIT facing court over student’s severed finger
canberra.snippet: The Canberra Institute of Technology is facing action from the work safety regulator over an incident at Floriade in which a student lost...
canberra.content:
Independent MLA Thomas Emerson says staff report serious safety concerns being ignored and dismissed. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The Canberra Institute of Technology is facing action from the work safety regulator over an incident at Floriade in which a student lost a finger.

CIT board member and chair of the audit and risk committee, Rose Jackson, revealed the incident during questioning by independent MLA Thomas Emerson, who later accused the struggling organisation of having a “cowboy culture”.

“Your question is about one that is with regard to a student whose finger was severed, and that work is continuing, and I’ll have to provide any more information on notice,” she said.

Ms Jackson later confirmed the incident occurred at Floriade.

The incident prompted a WorkSafe ACT investigation.

Ms Jackson confirmed that CIT was involved in a matter related to an enforceable undertaking to WorkSafe ACT, set down for hearing in the ACT Magistrates Court on 23 November.

A CIT spokesperson would only say that the organisation took the safety of students, staff, and visitors seriously.

“CIT won’t comment on individual matters,” the spokesperson said.

Mr Emerson said later that multiple current CIT staff had reached out with concerns about a “cowboy culture” at the Institute and that those who raised the issue faced recrimination.

“People who raise serious safety concerns report being ignored, dismissed and even targeted for having done so,” he said.

“I’ve received complaints from concerned CIT employees about senior officials acting like they’re ‘answerable to nobody’.”

Mr Emerson said that the current statutory and governance arrangements for CIT may have contributed to the situation.

“It’s very possible this culture has been fed by the establishment of an independent board back in 2015 and the related reduction in ministerial accountability and parliamentary scrutiny of what’s going on at CIT,” he said.

“This is something the government’s promised governance review needs to look at closely.”

Officials and Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson also fielded questions on the organisation’s cost-cutting plans, particularly the voluntary redundancy program.

Ms Jackson said a staff meeting was held on Tuesday morning (4 August) to explain the redundancy offer.

She said CIT was now waiting on responses, but the offer had been extended to all staff. There were no plans for forced redundancies.

When asked if this could result in fewer teachers, Ms Jackson said the goal was to “right-size” the organisation after years of declining student numbers.

“We are trying to deliver courses smarter, with regard to online, for example, rather than face-to-face, so all of those are being taken into consideration,” she said.

Applications for redundancy would be assessed based on staff roles and the capabilities they brought to CIT.

No decision has been made on how many voluntary redundancies will be issued, and the process could take up to 12 months, with offers staggered over time.

The offers would be funded through a combination of cash from the CIT budget and requests to the government for assistance.

Ms Jackson confirmed that the entire organisation was being overhauled.

“We’re going through a very large project of re-profiling the organisation, re-establishing what the best organisational structure that will work for CIT is,” she said.

Mr Pettersson said he had been advised of the redundancy program well in advance but was reluctant to say more.

“We’ve observed that this Assembly for many years, even preceding your time in this place, Mr Emerson, has made a range of recommendations about the size and composition of the CIT’s workforce,” he said.

“I see in the actions of the CIT board the responsiveness to those previous recommendations.”

The Sustainable Workforce Program could also include putting new hires and contract renewals on ice with all proposed vacancies, fixed-term contracts, contractor engagements and workshops under review.

canberra.title: ‘Uniquely Canberran’: Iconic bus shelters added to ACT Heritage Register
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s iconic precast concrete bus shelters have been added to the ACT Heritage Register, recognising their architectural, hist...
canberra.content:
4 August 2026

Join the conversation

3

The iconic bus shelters are instantly recognisable features of Canberra’s streetscapes. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra’s iconic precast concrete bus shelters have been added to the ACT Heritage Register, recognising their architectural, historic and social significance to the national capital.

Designed in 1975 by architect Clement (Clem) Cummings, the cream-and-orange shelters are instantly recognisable features of Canberra’s streetscape. There are more than 460 shelters across the city.

They were first installed in Canberra in May 1975 as part of a program to improve Canberra’s public transport system and address vandalism.

Council chair Catherine Skippington said the shelters are a distinctive example of Canberra’s planned urban development and design heritage.

“The bus shelters are uniquely Canberran. They are familiar landmarks in suburbs across the city and reflect the coordinated planning approach that helped shape Canberra as Australia’s planned national capital,” she said.

“Their Brutalist design is seen in their simple materials and modular forms, creating structures that are both practical and distinctive. They demonstrate how good public infrastructure can become part of a city’s identity.”

The ACT Heritage Council found the shelters were significant not only for their design qualities, but also for their strong community value and enduring role in Canberra’s suburban landscape.

Designed to be modular and relocatable, the shelters were intended to move with Canberra as it grew. Many have been relocated over time to serve new and expanding suburbs, a characteristic that remains an important part of their heritage significance.

The shelters were manufactured in Queanbeyan by Melocco. A total of 95 Series I design bus shelters were initially installed around Canberra city in 1975 at a cost of $2,300 per shelter, or a total of $218,500, equivalent to $1.8 million in 2024.

Since their introduction, the shelters have been painted cream, with orange fibreglass window frames and benches, to represent the sunset over the Brindabellas.

Following concerns about the initial cost of the shelters, Clem Cummings made minor amendments to the Series I design, with Series II featuring precast concrete floors, no backrests on bench seating, and no seats in shelters located near schools.

Five different series were produced. At least 170 additional shelters were installed throughout the 1980s and early 1990s.

Heritage registration does not change how the shelters are used, managed or maintained.

The registration recognises the shelters as an important part of Canberra’s modernist heritage and ensures their significance will be considered into the future.

Ms Skippington said the community response to the proposal demonstrated the strong connection Canberrans have with the shelters.

“The council was delighted by the overwhelmingly positive response received during public consultation. Many people described the shelters as ‘iconic’, ‘very Canberra’, and some shared personal anecdotes,” she said.

“We thank everyone who took the time to share their views, stories and memories. The feedback shows these iconic structures are woven into Canberra’s collective sense of place.”

The heritage registration takes effect once published on the ACT Legislation Register.

canberra.title: Next evolution of Ignite Cup builds momentum for Canberra-based NBL team
canberra.snippet: The next step in Canberra’s quest to secure a hometown NBL team has been taken, with the Capital securing the Ignite Cup Finals and...
canberra.content:
NBL great Cal Bruton and Sports Minister Chris Steel announcing Canberra has secured two major basketball events for 2027. Photo: ACT Government.

The next step in Canberra’s quest to secure a hometown NBL team has been taken, with the Capital securing the Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards.

The Hungry Jack’s National Basketball League (NBL) has confirmed the AIS Arena will host the tournament and the awards will be presented at Parliament House.

The four-team Ignite Cup Finals series will be held across two massive nights of basketball, with semi-finals on 19 February and a blockbuster decider on 21 February 2027.

NBL Group CEO David Stevenson said the Ignite Cup had quickly become one of the “standout innovations” in the NBL.

“Introducing a Final Four series and bringing it to Canberra is a fantastic evolution of the competition. Fans will experience a festival of basketball, with the best teams battling it out over one incredible weekend for the biggest prize pool in NBL history,” he said.

“Canberra has shown time and again that it embraces elite basketball. The incredible success of last year’s sold-out CODE Sports NBL Blitz proved there’s a huge appetite for the game, and we’re excited to build on that momentum by bringing the Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards to the nation’s capital.”

The Ignite Cup features 20 Wednesday night games, with results counting towards the regular-season ladder, as teams compete for a share of $400,000 in prize money.

NBL great Andrew Gaze said Canberra used to be home to the “mecca” of all basketball venues in the country.

He hoped the work underway on planning and detailed design for Canberra’s new National Convention and Entertainment Centre would help make the Territory once again a hub for basketball.

“Some absolute superstars have played here … but let’s not forget about the grassroots, because the grassroots here in Canberra and the talent they’re producing need more courts,” Mr Gaze said.

“There’s a lot of people that want to participate at all different levels, and when that base is strong, the elite becomes even better.”

Alongside the ACT’s $31.1 million commitment to progress planning and detailed design for Canberra’s new National Convention and Entertainment Centre, the 2027 Ignite Cup Finals also provides momentum towards a possible Canberra-based NBL team.

Mr Stevenson said discussions were still afoot about when that would happen, but this was another great step.

“I think we’re building a really strong business case, and it’s not just about what happens at the game; it’s the economic contribution … the amount of people who are coming from interstate,” he said.

“We’ve had an incredible success story out of the Jack Jumpers down in Tasmania – our last expansion team – [they] sold out every single game they’ve ever played, so we’ve got a strong confidence that we can work together … to make sure that, hopefully, once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team.”

NBL great Andrew Gaze, Chief Minister Andrew Barr and Sports Minister Chris Steel are keen for the events to further grow Canberra’s basketball offerings. Photo: ACT Government.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr agreed that strong economic growth was expected from these two events.

“It is a strategic investment that supports not only our T2030 goal of growing visitor spend by $1 billion by 2030, but also our 2024 election commitment to work with the NBL on bringing elite men’s basketball back to Canberra,” he said.

“Bringing the 2027 Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards to our city means the entire NBL family – from players, officials, and fans from every club – will be here for a full weekend.

“The Ignite Cup Finals will fill our hotels, restaurants, cafes and bars, supporting local jobs and giving our accommodation and hospitality sectors a fantastic boost.”

The Andrew Gaze MVP awards will be presented from the Great Hall in Parliament House.

It will bring the entire League together and help promote Canberra’s unique and exclusive event locations.

It’s the first time the Awards have been presented outside of Melbourne in more than a decade.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said bringing both events to Canberra would further enhance the city’s reputation as a destination for major sporting events.

“Events like this inspire the next generation to get involved in the sport and in February Canberrans can watch their sporting heroes compete right here in their own city,” he said.

“Canberrans love their basketball, and it’s great to see the NBL backing that in. What a fantastic outcome for the ACT.”

Fans are encouraged to pre-register for tickets, with the full Finals program to be released during the season.

canberra.title: Woman who allegedly killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown denies dangerous driving
canberra.snippet: A woman has been committed to a higher court for trial over a crash that killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown. NSW Police previously said...
canberra.content:
4 August 2026

Jackie McKeown was killed in a crash in November 2024. Photo: VisitCanberra LinkedIn.

A woman has been committed to a higher court for trial over a crash that killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown.

NSW Police previously said that Ms McKeown was walking along Bicentennial Drive in Jerrabomberra on the morning of 17 November 2024 when a ute hit her.

Paramedics arrived and began CPR, but the 48-year-old died at the scene.

The ute’s alleged driver, the then-54-year-old Teresa Anne McDonald, suffered broken ribs and facial injuries in the crash.

She was taken to hospital for treatment and mandatory testing.

In the aftermath of her death, members of Canberra’s tourism community released tributes to Ms McKeown.

She had worked as the Canberra and Region Visitors Centre’s director of visitor services for the three years before her death.

In May 2025, Ms McDonald was charged with dangerous driving occasioning death and negligent driving occasioning death.

At the time, a NSW Police spokesperson said her licence was also suspended following the alleged offending.

On Monday (4 August), she formally pleaded not guilty to dangerous driving occasioning death, as well as an alternative charge of negligent driving occasioning death.

Ms McDonald is next scheduled to face the NSW District Court on 9 September.

canberra.title: The Lager House has found its groove and already feels like an old favourite
canberra.snippet: Nearly six months after opening its doors, Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled comfortably. It seems like the right time to see...
canberra.content:
Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled in, and it’s an official winner with Canberrans. Photo: Lager House.

Nearly six months after opening its doors, Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled comfortably. It seems like the right time to see how this sleeker interpretation of Capital’s well-established Canberra presence was shaping up.

If turning up on a Tuesday night in the middle of winter and only just managing to snag the last available table is any indication, it’s official: Canberra has fallen hard for its newest neighbourhood pub.

And there’s plenty to love here.

Capital Brewing has traded the industrial, brewpub feel of the Tap Room on Dairy Road for something more polished, but without sacrificing the approachability that made the original a Canberra favourite. The higher-end finishes, moody lighting and lofty ceilings take the experience up a notch, while the atmosphere remains relaxed, friendly and unmistakably local.

Specialty side-pour beer taps were imported from Europe for the perfect pour at Lager House. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Much like the decor, the beer offering also departs from its predecessor, with one obvious difference being the volume.

Dairy Road has around 20 drinks on tap, including beers, wines, ginger beers and cider. The Lager House has around half of that, but with the focus on their four rotating tank-fresh beers, which not only look sexy with the massive stainless steel tanks living on the pub floor, but also offer a more consistent pour so you always get the perfect beer.

I’m glad to see that, since opening, they’ve added a mid-strength beer to the tap line-up, allowing non-locals to still have a nice time and drive home safely at the end of it. Good Drop is a damn good lager, so it deserves a place on the taps.

Another glaring departure from Dairy Road is that the Brodburger partnership hasn’t carried over to the Lager House; instead, they’ve gone all in on their own woodfired kitchen, and this is what I really wanted to dive into while I sipped on my roasty, toasty, malty dark lager amusingly called All Night Long.

Bringing the food in-house has paid off. The menu is seasonal, delivering on the big bold flavours that you want at a pub while offering variety outside of your usual pub grub offerings.

The barramundi was a little lost under all the parsley but delicious nonetheless. Photo: Martin Conway.

The crispy-skinned barramundi at $34 is flame-roasted, sits atop a bed of romesco and olives, and is topped with almonds. My fish was cooked to perfection, moist and flaky with crispy skin. The use of parsley was a little heavy-handed for my taste, crossing the line from garnish to blanket, burying the whole dish under its foliage, but it was easily pushed aside.

The woodfired chicken skewers at $32 are served like a deconstructed kebab with tabbouleh, tzatziki, hummus, flatbread and chimichurri on the side. Assembling it into little bite-sized parcels to pop in your mouth seemed like the best approach, and it delivered on flavour, reminiscent of your favourite Turkish kebab joint.

The chicken skewers take your favourite kebab and deconstruct it. Photo: Martin Conway.

The surprise hero of the meal was the crispy Brussels sprouts with hot honey and toasted almonds. At $15, this is a generous serve and a wonderful blend of flavours and textures that had us dragging our fingers through the remaining hot honey, only sheepishly withdrawing as the server came to collect our plate.

For those better organised than me, you can go deeper into the woodfired menu by pre-ordering a dish from the woodfired feasts menu, which needs to be arranged at least 24 hours in advance. The feasts are designed for sharing and include rib-eye, lamb shoulder, crispy pork knuckle, miso-glazed pumpkin and charred cabbage.

The overall experience, while a departure from what you already know and love, holds onto the core of what made Capital so good in the first place. It’s like an old friend who has had a glow-up, but is as cool as ever.

Lager House by Capital Brewing Co is located at 62 Constitution Avenue, Campbell, and is open 7 days a week from 11:30 am.

australia.content:
Minns government will not implement recommendation of long-awaited hate speech report

Penry Buckley

The NSW government will not expand a controversial offence for inciting hatred to include religion, sexual orientation or gender identity, against the recommendation of a report which it has been sitting on for eight months.

In a statement this afternoon, the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, said the government was today releasing the report by former supreme court justice John Sackar, first provided to the government in November.

In the report, Sackar has recommended that section 93ZAA of the NSW Crimes Act, an offence for inciting hatred on the grounds of race, brought in last year against the recommendation of the NSW Law Reform Commission, be “amended to included all attributes currently protected by section 93Z”.

Section 93Z, the offence for inciting violence, covers offences committed on the basis of someone’s race, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity or intersex or HIV/Aids status.

Daley said:

After careful consideration of the Sackar Review and its recommendations, the NSW Government has decided not to expand the existing criminal offence of inciting racial hatred to apply to additional protected attributes.

There is no place for hatred in NSW. Everyone deserves to feel safe, respected and free from intimidation, regardless of their background, faith, sexuality or identity.

The Government’s view is that expanding the racial hatred offence to cover other attributes raises complex questions about freedom of expression, freedom of religion, and the consistent application of the criminal law across the community.”

NSW government accused of denying LGBTQ+ communities equal protection after rejecting Sackar report key recommendation

The Minns government has been accused of denying LGBTQ+ communities equal protection from hate after announcing it would not implement a key recommendation from a report it sat on for 8 months.

The NSW government released the long-awaited report on Tuesday and announced it would not expand a controversial offence and criminalise inciting hatred on the grounds of religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.

This went against a key recommendation of the report, which was written by former supreme court justice, John Sackar, and recommended that section 93ZAA of the NSW Crimes Act, which criminalises inciting hatred on the grounds of race, be expanded.

Equality Australia said of the decision:

The government said that expanding the existing racial hatred offence to cover other attributes raised complex questions about freedom of expression and religion.

The government has already shown it can balance these rights when it comes to racial hatred.

Claiming that the same approach cannot apply to other communities is disingenuous, creating an inconsistent legal framework and a hierarchy of protections.

Penry Buckley

Witness claims Dominic Perrottet knew brother was in Fiji during parliamentary inquiry, watchdog hears

The NSW Liberal shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, has concluded giving his evidence to the Icac’s Operation Rosny.

In the latter stages, questioning from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, focused on a parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s current inquiry.

The inquiry has heard last week that Jean-Claude Perrottet, brother of the then Liberal premier, Dominic Perrottet, travelled to Fiji to avoid appearing before the parliamentary inquiry, which was not known publicly at the time.

Tudehope has admitted to discussing the details of Jean-Claude’s location with Dominic Perrottet:

I did have a discussion with Dom at one stage, and it was a very casual discussion … I just said, ‘Where is Jean-Claude?’ And he said he didn’t know. But then, on a subsequent discussion, I think he may have told me he was in Fiji.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing, while Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Senior NSW Liberal admits to leaking confidential report to Reformers

Penry Buckley

Returning to the NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny:

The shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, has admitted to leaking a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a member of the Reformers.

Tudehope was asked if he could recall coming into possession of a confidential draft copy of the inquiry’s report in February 2023, when the Liberals were still in government. He said he could not, but said he was aware of the obligation to keep a draft report confidential.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, was shown an email in which he had sent the report as an attachment to Reformer Jeremy Greenwood.

Dwyer: Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?

Tudehope: It appears that I did.

Dwyer: Why did you do that?

Tudehope: Oh well, I thought he would have had an interest in that report.

Dwyer: What was your purpose in providing it to Mr Greenwood?

Tudehope: Its contents.

Asked what his purpose was in providing the report to Greenwood, Tudehope said he did not know what Greenwood did when he received it, and does not know if he would have shared it with fellow Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet. “That would have been a decision for him,” said Tudehope.

Melissa Davey

Carers and advocates give evidence at Support at Home inquiry

The Senate Community Affairs Committee inquiry into aged care Support at Home reforms heard evidence of lengthy waits for assessments and funding, reduced access to care, and a growing burden placed on unpaid carers.

Dementia Australia advocate Lynda Henderson, a key participant in a working group established by the Department of Health to advise on the reforms told the inquiry she felt “personally cheated” by the decision to use algorithms to determine funding outcomes, without any capacity for human override.

She said the survey known as the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) was designed to support clinicians in assessing individual needs, not to replace the professional judgement of qualified assessors.

Guardian Australia previously reported Henderson’s story and the impact of the IAT, which is underpinned by an algorithm to determine government funding.

“I now feel personally cheated as well as horrified by the numbers of incorrect assessment results produced by these algorithms and the consequences of those,” Henderson told the inquiry.

Representatives from Dementia Australia told the committee in their submission that “a national crisis is unfolding in Australia’s aged care system”.

Their national survey found 94% of professionals reported dementia-related needs were not being fully captured through the assessment process.

Shadow health minister Senator Anne Ruston said; “Every story we have heard reinforces that aged care cannot be reduced to forms, queues and computer-generated decisions”.

Read more:

Independent review of Bureau of Meteorology announced

Donna Lu

The chief executive of the Bureau of Meteorology has commissioned an independent review of the agency, to “ensure it delivers value to Australians in a rapidly changing environment”.

In November, the BoM publicly apologised for how it handled its new website launch – the first redesign in a decade. Guardian Australia revealed that the full cost of the website overhaul was approximately $86m, which came after years of delays and millions in cost blowouts.

That followed an attempted rebrand in 2022, and allegations of a toxic workplace culture.

The review, which will inform the BoM’s next strategic plan, to come into effect in late 2027, will assess the “effectiveness of public communications and responsiveness to stakeholder needs”.

The environment minister, Murray Watt, said the review would “bring an independent perspective to understanding the services being delivered and how that value can be strengthened into the future”.

The BoM chief executive, Dr Stuart Minchin, said the review would help the agency “better understand current and future customer needs”, adding:

Our work underpins essential services, economic activity, environmental health and community wellbeing, for all Australians every day, so it’s important we get it right.

A report by the review panel is expected by 31 March.

Andrew Messenger

More than 1,500 Brisbane children experienced homelessness in past year

At least 1,539 children from 984 families are known to have spent time homeless in Brisbane in the last year.

The statistics were collated by Brisbane Zero, a collaboration between 28 government and non-government organisations.

About 40% of the almost exclusively female-led households became homeless as a result of relationship breakdown; 38% due to violence at home. The average age of the head of household was 25; 72% had experienced at least one health or substance abuse issue in the last year.

The numbers only include homeless people who are known by name.

Acting chief executive officer of Micah Projects Bridget Kinch said the statistics were heading in the wrong direction. She said:

I think the housing crisis, the unaffordability for people, I think there’s a lack of housing pathways for people.

I think we’ve seen that improve in the first half of this year, so it’s great to see that happening but the concern is where’s the rest of the stock or the places for people.

In the past year 2,326 individuals experienced homelessness, 985 of them for the first time. In that time 261 of them found housing, with 90 returning to homelessness from housing.

Several homeless people also died in Brisbane in the last year, though they are not included on the list.

Penry Buckley

NSW hate speech report released after lengthy parliamentary battle

Following on from our previous post:

The release of the Sackar report at the start of a busy sitting week and in the middle of a landmark Icac inquiry into corruption in the NSW Liberal party comes after a long-running battle to have the report released by the opposition and crossbench.

The premier, Chris Minns, had refused to release it before the cabinet made a policy decision, amid growing speculation about what it contained.

Earlier this year, the NSW upper house passed a unanimous motion, unopposed by Labor, under a procedure known as standing order 52 (SO52), which requires the government to release documents.

The government returned a five-page document, containing five letters from senior public servants and chiefs of staff in the premier’s, attorney general’s and police minister’s offices, all of them certifying that “no documents covered by the terms of the resolution and lawfully required to be provided are held by The Cabinet Office or the Premier’s Department”.

The upper house subsequently voted to suspend Labor minister John Graham. More recently, it sought legal advice about whether the document was in fact “cabinet in confidence”.

The NSW government will not expand a controversial offence for inciting hatred to include religion, sexual orientation or gender identity, against the recommendation of a report which it has been sitting on for eight months.

In a statement this afternoon, the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, said the government was today releasing the report by former supreme court justice John Sackar, first provided to the government in November.

In the report, Sackar has recommended that section 93ZAA of the NSW Crimes Act, an offence for inciting hatred on the grounds of race, brought in last year against the recommendation of the NSW Law Reform Commission, be “amended to included all attributes currently protected by section 93Z”.

Section 93Z, the offence for inciting violence, covers offences committed on the basis of someone’s race, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity or intersex or HIV/Aids status.

Daley said:

After careful consideration of the Sackar Review and its recommendations, the NSW Government has decided not to expand the existing criminal offence of inciting racial hatred to apply to additional protected attributes.

There is no place for hatred in NSW. Everyone deserves to feel safe, respected and free from intimidation, regardless of their background, faith, sexuality or identity.

The Government’s view is that expanding the racial hatred offence to cover other attributes raises complex questions about freedom of expression, freedom of religion, and the consistent application of the criminal law across the community.”

EV sales, air travel drive rebound in consumer spending

Australian households show no sign of pulling back on spending despite the Middle East conflict exacerbating cost-of-living concerns, AAP reports.

Strong growth in electric vehicle purchases and a bounce back in air travel drove a surprisingly strong 0.8% increase in household spending in June, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Analysts had been expecting a rise of just 0.2% in the month.

Spending growth was driven by a 3% rise in transport spending in the month, where new vehicle sales stood out.

The ABS head of business statistics, Tom Lay, said:

Electric vehicle sales increased significantly over the year and have continued that trend in June, accounting for a growing share of overall new vehicles sales as households adjust their spending behaviour in response to rising fuel prices.

EV sales doubled in the space of three months as the Middle East conflict disrupted oil supplies and sent fuel prices soaring, the Australian Automobile Association said on Sunday.

Lower fuel prices in June also supported spending on air travel, which returned to pre-Iran war levels.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take things from here. Take care.

Victorian doctors to go on strike for first time in 20 years

The Australian Medical Association Victoria branch said doctors will engage in a stop-work action on Thursday 13 August, affecting hospitals across the Melbourne CBD and in Parkville. It’s the first time doctors have taken protected industrial action in the area in 20 years.

The action, centred on a pay dispute, will occur from 12.30pm to 4pm alongside some statewide actions across all health services. Hospitals affected include the Royal Melbourne hospital and the Royal Children’s and Women’s hospitals.

AMA Victoria said the industrial action had been carefully designed to protect patient care, with a spokesperson adding:

Participating doctors will work with their hospitals to ensure appropriate arrangements are in place so that patient care is not compromised.

Many doctors will remain working instead of taking industrial action specifically so that their colleagues can participate in the action without compromising patient care.

Doctors working in emergency departments and those in other, critical frontline services will not participate in the stop-work action.

AMA Victoria president Simon Judkins told the ABC doctors had tried to negotiate a better pay deal for a year, saying many had reported “incredibly high levels of fatigue and stress, and they’re incredibly worried in those conditions about whether they might be prone to making errors”.

Nino Bucci

Antisemitism royal commission hearing evidence about police, protests

The royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion has resumed public hearings, with the next block of evidence to focus on protests and policing.

Richard Lancaster SC, counsel assisting justice Virginia Bell, said the hearing would focus on protests held outside the Sydney Opera House on 9 October 2023 and by neo-Nazis outside NSW parliament on 8 November 2025.

Lancaster said multiple people had told the commission that the Opera House protest was “a critical event in the rise of antisemitism” in Australia.

He said one witness told the commission it was “shattering of our physical and psychological sense of safety in this country” a sentiment “echoed by many other Jewish Australians”.

Lancaster also said there was a large body of evidence before the commission showing that protesting against Israeli military action in Gaza or showing humanitarian concern for civilians killed in the Middle East conflict was not antisemitic.

The first witness, David Ossip, the president of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, said he respected the right of people to protest in support of Palestine.

But he said the timing of the rally, which started at Sydney town hall before ending at the Opera House, was insensitive, given the events of 7 October.

Acting deputy commissioner of NSW police, Peter McKenna, said that while he understood the “heightened emotions” regarding conduct at the rally, there were no concerns about community safety. He said:

When I spoke to police on the ground, they did not have a concern that this protest would get out of control.

The hearing continues.

Charity cyclist who just finished 5,200km MND fundraising ride dies aged 82

Bob Montgomery, a charity cyclist who recently finished a 5,200km bike ride from Broome to Bowral, died on Monday at the age of 82.

His family confirmed his death on social media, saying he had died unexpectedly just a day after completing the cycling feat as a fundraiser for motor neurone disease, alongside his grandson, Tom. They wrote:

This was Bob’s sixth interstate fundraising ride in support of Motor Neurone Disease NSW, raising vital funds and awareness for a cause that was deeply personal to him. Fittingly, and now poignantly, the ride was named One Last Ride.

At 82 years of age, Bob was still passionately sharing his message only hours before his passing.

MND NSW shared a tribute saying the body was “deeply saddened” by the sudden passing, calling Montgomery a “cherished friend and tireless supporter of MND NSW”.

The group’s CEO, Liam O’Meara, said in a statement:

For many years, Bob dedicated himself to raising vital funds and awareness for people living with motor neurone disease. His most recent achievement, riding from Broome to Bowral at the age of 82 alongside his 18-year-old grandson, was nothing short of inspirational.

Bob understood that behind every diagnosis is a person and a family navigating one of life’s most challenging journeys. His fundraising helped ensure that more people could access the care, equipment and support they need, when they need it most.

Australian shares surge to five-month high

Australia’s share market is trading at a five-month high, led by a strong rally by the major banks and a subdued oil price, AAP reports.

The S&P/ASX200 jumped 114.7 points by midday, up 0.28%, to 9,134.8, as the broader All Ordinaries gained 120.2 points, or 1.31%, to 9,298.6.

The top-200 came within 66 points of its 9,202.9 record peak set in February, as the local bourse tracked a strong Wall Street on hopes the US and Iran would restart diplomatic efforts to solve the Persian Gulf conflict.

australia.title: NSW Liberal admits to leaking confidential report to young conservative powerbrokers, inquiry hears
australia.snippet: NSW shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, tells inquiry Jean-Claude Perrottet had a talent for recruiting The leader of the oppositio...
australia.content:
The leader of the opposition in the New South Wales upper house has admitted to leaking a confidential draft report from a 2023 parliamentary inquiry to a member of a group of young conservative Liberal powerbrokers now under investigation by the corruption watchdog, an inquiry has heard.

On Tuesday, Damien Tudehope, the NSW shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house, gave evidence as part of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny.

The inquiry is investigating allegations the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations to recruit or renew members to the party, a practice known as branch stacking, which is not itself illegal.

Tudehope, who has stood aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry, is not named in any allegations by Icac.

On Tuesday afternoon, counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC, asked Tudehope about a parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe. Tudehope had been the leader of the government in the upper house, under then-Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, until February 2023.

Tudehope was asked if he could recall coming into possession of a confidential draft copy of the inquiry’s report in that month. He said he could not, but was aware of the obligation to keep a draft parliamentary report confidential.

He was shown an email in which he had sent the report as an attachment to Reformer Jeremy Greenwood. Dwyer asked: “Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?”

“It appears that I did,” said Tudehope.

The inquiry has heard that Reformers Greenwood, Christian Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of Dominic Perrottet, avoided appearing at the inquiry. Under questioning from Dwyer, Tudehope claimed to have had discussions on Jean-Claude’s whereabouts with Dominic Perrottet.

“I did have a discussion with Dom at one stage, and it was a very casual discussion ... I just said, ‘Where is Jean-Claude?’ And he said he didn’t know. But then, in a subsequent discussion, I think he may have told me he was in Fiji,” he said.

Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing. At the time of the parliamentary inquiry, Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, rejected allegations his brother had tried to orchestrate a branch-stacking operation to unseat federal Coalition MP Alex Hawke, saying “leave my family out of it”.

On Tuesday, Icac heard evidence from businessman Frits Maré, the key witness at the parliamentary inquiry, about a 2020 meeting in which Perrottet and Christian Ellis asked him to contribute $50,000 to an operation to unseat Hawke.

Tudehope, whose name has been mentioned frequently during the first two weeks of hearings, gave evidence about the time Jean-Claude Perrottet and Christian Ellis spent in his electorate and ministerial offices.

He admitted that Jean-Claude Perrottet had a “talent” for recruiting and renewing new members to the party, which he said was essential for any Liberal member looking to hold their seat at preselection.

“[Jean-Claude] had a fairly wide connection of friends, which he was able to marshal together and exploit. Which is well, I won’t say exploit, but sort of get to do things for him.”

Jean-Claude worked in Tudehope’s electorate office in 2018 and in his parliamentary office in 2019, when Tudehope was minister for finance.

Asked about a 2018 message in which Jean-Claude wrote to other Reformers that “Scott and Damien are afraid”. Recognising “Scott” as the former head of his electorate office, Tudehope said he did not recall raising concerns or being aware that Jean-Claude may have been using his hours as an electorate officer in recruiting Liberal members, although it may have “potentially arisen”.

Tudehope described a later incident in which his chief of staff “blew up” about a newspaper article about staffers spending ministerial hours on recruitment against their code of conduct.

The inquiry heard that Ellis was only employed as a staffer in Tudehope’s ministerial office for three months before being terminated in July 2019. Tudehope said that the article “was probably the precipitating event” for Ellis’s dismissal.

The Reformers, who were part of same the conservative right faction as Tudehope, wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia. Tudehope, who admitted to speaking at multiple Reformers recruitment events, defended himself as “a warrior for social issues for the party”.

After being shown evidence of a bank transfer and one message from Jean-Claude in which he wrote that “Damien” had paid for a venue for an event, and another – “Damien got it” – which suggested he had contributed $5,000 for a Reformers table at a right faction event, Tudehope admitted he may have made payments to the Reformers.

His son, James Tudehope, is not named in allegations but has declined a request to give evidence to Icac after moving to New Zealand earlier this year.

Tudehope told the inquiry on Tuesday that his son, while an employee of Catholic Schools NSW, had raised concerns “at a Sunday lunch” about payments allegedly being made by the schools governing body to Beckington, a lobbying company controlled by Ellis.

“He said to me that, ‘I’m being pressured to pay an invoice for Christian Ellis, and I just don’t think we should be paying it’.”

Tudehope’s former business partner , hotelier Michael O’Hara, is alleged to have made political donations to the Reformers, prohibited because of his involvement in the liquor and gambling industries.

Under questioning from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, Tudehope accepted that he introduced Reformers Ellis and Robert Assaf to O’Hara and that he was aware O’Hara was “generous” and would be likely to support their factional work financially.

But like O’Hara, the inquiry’s first witness last week, Tudehope disputed whether payments to the Reformers, who were not a registered party, would count as political donations.

“If you think that I would expose a friend of mine to that level of scrutiny that he was exposed to, 83 years of age with stage ... four cancer, do you think that I would have done that in circumstances where I knew that he would be a prohibited donor for the purposes of the Electoral Funding Act? Not on your life.”

Before Tudehope’s evidence on Tuesday afternoon, the NSW Liberal Leader, Kellie Sloane, told reporters at a morning press conference she believed there was a “pathway back” for Tudehope to her frontbench.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: Alan Jones paid student athlete he is accused of indecently assaulting $110,000 over a decade, trial hears
australia.snippet: Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty Alan Jo...
australia.content:
A student athlete who received more than $110,000 from Alan Jones over a decade has told a Sydney court he reported indecent assaults to police after the broadcaster was arrested in 2024 because he wanted his child to know “right from wrong”.

“I feel like I’m here because of being unable to say no,” the man, known as complainant J, told Downing Centre local court on Tuesday.

The alleged victim, who met Jones when he was 14, said he was “disappointed” in himself for failing to stand up to Jones and the alleged abuse.

“I’m a father now, and I’m a proud father, and I want to teach my [child] right from wrong and what he was doing was wrong,” J said on day two of Jones’s trial on 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges. Jones has pleaded not guilty.

The complainant, now in his 40s, earlier on Tuesday told the court details of alleged indecent assaults at Jones’s farm in Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands when he was 17.

J said that, over a glass of wine after dinner, Jones told him: “There is only one rule here: There are no rules.”

J told the court that the broadcaster later allegedly said: “Go and have a shower and come out wearing a robe and nothing else.”

Asked by the crown prosecutor Georgina Wright if he followed those instructions, J said: “No, I put my underpants on, and then I put the robe on and went out.” Jones was in a room with a grand piano, the court heard.

Wright asked J: “Why did you put the underpants on?”

“I almost knew what was going to happen,” J replied. “Easy access. He’s going to touch me.”

J alleged Jones was sitting on the lounge, also in a robe, and was drinking a glass of wine.

J alleged that Jones “looked me straight in the eye” and stated in a “quiet”, “calm” and “sympathising tone”: “I said the robe and nothing.”

The alleged victim told the court that Jones then “put his hand back on my penis and started rubbing it”.

Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.

Jones’s defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC on Monday argued the alleged victims were egged on to complain by media rivals, and their reliability and credibility were questionable.

This included, Bashir alleged, shockjock Ray Hadley and Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons.

J on Tuesday told the court that later that same evening in Fitzroy Falls, he and Jones watched TV and discussed sport.

The then-teenager mentioned he was getting tired and said he was going to bed, J told the court.

After J went to his room, he alleged that he heard a “tap, tap, tap”, and Jones came into the room.

“He said ‘Is everything OK [J]?’” J alleged Jones came closer and said in a “really passionate voice … ‘I love you mate’ and pulled me in for a cuddle”.

He alleged that Jones “groped” him on the bum and “it was aggressive”.

“While I was being held by the buttocks, he reached around and undid my robe, and he pulled my underpants down a quarter way down my legs,” J told the court.

“He started to wiggle his body so our penises would cross and touch each other.

“There was a slight opportunity where the grip … was released … I was able to step back and sat on the bed, and said I was going to go to bed.”

J alleged that Jones then walked to the other side of the bed.

“My heart was racing. I was as scared and nervous as I had been in a long time. It was that feeling when you go into a room you’ve never been in, like a scary room, my heart felt like it was going to come out of my chest.

“The defendant placed his hand on my penis and began to squeeze it tight and release it. I was frozen.”

J alleged that Jones then said “let’s come together” and they both masturbated.

“I thought if I do this, and I just do it myself, it can be over … and would prevent him from doing it or being near me or touching me. I thought it was the quickest way to make it over and done with, and that’s what happened.”

J told the court he did not consent to what unfolded in the room.

J said he watched Jones’s arrest on television almost two years ago, and he contacted the police station where Jones was taken. J was put in contact with a detective and made a statement, he told the court.

“People need me to do this,” he said on Tuesday. “It’s the right thing to do.”

J said he did not want money, and he would not pursue Jones for compensation in a civil court. “I just want justice,” he told the court.

Under cross-examination by defence barrister Bashir, J said he had not read articles by Kate McClymont that were published in the Sydney Morning Herald before Jones’s arrest.

“I am not sure who that is,” J said.

J repeatedly disagreed with Bashir when she put to him that he had read details about other alleged indecent assaults in the press before making a statement to the police.

“I don’t read newspapers,” J said. He said he did not have a subscription to the Sydney Morning Herald.

“It’s my evidence that I haven’t read or seen any of the specifics,” J said. “I have never read any of this.”

The trial continues.

australia.title: Trump wants ‘fair treatment’ in fight over Labor’s levy on tech giants to pay for news, US trade group warns
australia.snippet: National Foreign Trade Council ‘disappointed’ at move to expand News Bargaining Incentive but Australian experts say government is not go...
australia.content:
A major US trade body has rubbished the Albanese government’s plan to make more big tech platforms pay for Australian journalism, issuing a veiled warning about how Donald Trump may respond to the “deteriorating trend”.

The National Foreign Trade Council said it was “disappointed” at the Australian government’s move to expand its News Bargaining Incentive (NBI) to take in Microsoft’s LinkedIn, amid trade tensions between Washington and Canberra including newly increased tariffs on Australian goods.

But competition experts in Australia say the government has not gone far enough in helping support news outlets whose content is being exploited by platforms such as Facebook and Google, and that the exclusion of AI platforms was a major flaw.

“I hope they move on the AI issue and give us that clarity,” said the former ACCC chair Rod Sims.

“I’d like to see a bit of urgency. The potential lack of ambition, and not every [media outlet] getting a deal, certainly worries me.”

The proposed NBI, which the Albanese government seeks to legislate in coming months, would require tech giants to compensate media outlets for the news on their platforms, either through making commercial deals or paying a higher levy.

It initially included Google, TikTok and Meta; Monday’s announcement that the NBI would include professional networking sites – previously carved out from the plan – and increase the cost charge but reduce the cost base, was hailed by Labor as a fairer model.

But Tiffany Smith, the vice-president of global trade policy at the National Foreign Trade Council, criticised the move.

“We remain disappointed that Australia continues to push forward with a news bargaining incentive that now covers an even broader spectrum of US companies,” she told Guardian Australia.

The NFTC is a major American trade lobby, with members including affected companies Meta, Microsoft and Google; other tech companies such as Amazon, Apple and Samsung; and major firms like BP, Coca-Cola, Ford, Toyota, Shell and Visa.

“The Trump administration has made it clear that it is fully committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad. We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” Smith said.

But Sims, a former boss of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a supporter of the NBI, said the government wasn’t doing enough to support news.

Under the plan, big tech platforms would have to make at least six individual deals with news publishers – up from a previous four – to avoid paying the levy, set at a higher rate.

The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, who is leading the process, said on Monday that Australian media would expect to receive “$200 million to $250 million” in total under the arrangements.

Sims said he was pleased the NBI was progressing, and would scrap the carve out for professional networking sites, but said more money should be raised to support journalism – noting $250m was the figure raised under the former News Media Bargaining Code, legislated by the Coalition half a decade ago, and which only included Meta and Google.

Sims said the government should be aiming higher than that, more in the realm of $300m plus, with more companies included and inflation added.

“There’s a lack of ambition, and simple arithmetic here,” Sims said.

News Corp’s Australian chair, Michael Miller, claimed the government’s changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media”, saying the rules “need strengthening, not softening”.

“On an already uneven playing field, getting this wrong won’t just hurt Australian media. It will erode the quality and independence of news every Australian relies on,” he said.

The changes were also criticised by the Coalition and Greens, making the NBI’s pathway through parliament unclear when the legislation is introduced in coming weeks.

Sims was critical that AI platforms deriving value from Australian news would not be captured – even those incorporated into NBI-exposed companies, such as Google’s Gemini. He also worried that many outlets would miss out on benefit, with big tech companies only obliged to make six deals minimum.

“It just means not everybody will get a deal, in fact most won’t … some outlets in public interest journalism won’t get some. That’s a real concern,” he said.

Another former ACCC chair, Allan Fels, said it was positive the government was making progress, but worried the scheme didn’t go far enough to “extract more from the platforms” for Australian journalism.

A Microsoft spokesperson said the company “shares the Government’s objective of promoting a sustainable Australian news ecosystem” and said it would continue “constructive engagement with Government, publishers and industry stakeholders to support high-quality journalism, innovation and economic growth”.

world.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says
world.snippet: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people The president of the Eu...
world.content:
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.

In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”

She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spanish officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌with Morocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.

Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave in north Africa on Thursday. Authorities in Ceuta reported that 88 people died trying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land borders with Africa. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.

EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.

She said the EU should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

Italian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently said risked becoming “human rights black holes”.

The EU opened the door to offshore detention centres in June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.

Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.

The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s leader isolated.

Over the weekend, Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest” and contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.

Italy and Denmark organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision to regularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.

EU member states favouring a tough approach to migration are expected to raise the issue of “pull factors” on Tuesday. “There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2 million people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open,” an EU diplomat said, referring to the approximate number of people who applied for regularisation under the 2026 Spanish government programme.

Academic research has found no evidence of a pull effect from regularisation programmes on arrivals of irregular migrants.

Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”

Amid widespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.

Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but which have been heavily criticised by rights groups.

Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”

Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”
